summary.text: A 9-day-old male neonate with a prenatally identified paternally inherited heterozygous COL1A2 c.1459G > A (p.Gly487Arg) mutation, born by cesarean section at 34 weeks after prenatal ultrasound findings suggestive of OI, was transferred to the NICU in January 2025 for persistent respiratory distress. He had tachypnea of 56 breaths per minute, retractions, thoracoabdominal asynchrony, bilateral rales, oxygen saturation declining to 85%, bilateral knee valgus deformities and lower limb bowing, with non-blue sclerae, elevated interleukin-6 and normal calcium, phosphate and ALP. Sanger sequencing confirmed the mutation and skeletal survey radiographs showed generalized osteopenia, thin cortices and bowing. Normal calcium, phosphate and ALP helped rule out metabolic bone disease.

He was diagnosed with neonatal pneumonia, preterm infant status and OI Sillence type III and managed with a multidisciplinary protocol: nCPAP (PEEP 5 cmH_(2)O, FiO_(2) 30%) instead of immediate intubation, later reduced to HFNC and discontinued on day 18 of life; handle-with-care nursing protocols; and oral Vitamin AD, calcium gluconate, mixed feeding and parenteral nutrition. Respiratory support was weaned as pneumonia resolved, with full enteral feeding and no new fractures during the 9-day hospitalization, and he was discharged at a corrected gestational age of 36 weeks +5 days. nCPAP stabilized his respiration, avoiding invasive mechanical ventilation.

On the 16th day after discharge (25th day of life) he had a spontaneous fracture of the right proximal femur, managed conservatively with a Pavlik harness after consultation with the pediatric orthopedic team. Radiographs at 52 days of age showed abundant callus formation with blurred fracture lines, and by 136 days of age radiographic union with completed remodeling was confirmed, with the underlying bony abnormalities persisting.

caption_evidence.quote:
Figure 2
Sanger sequencing confirmation of the COL1A2 mutation in the proband. Postnatal Sanger sequencing validation confirmed the presence of the heterozygous c.1459G > A mutation (red arrow) in the proband's peripheral blood DNA. This missense mutation leads to the substitution of glycine by arginine at position 487 (p.Gly487Arg) within the highly conserved triple-helical domain of the collagen α2(I) chain. Such structural mutations are typically associated with a severe type III OI phenotype.

caption_evidence.quote:
Figure 7
Radiographic evidence of rapid fracture healing (day 52 of life). Follow-up radiograph of the right femur reveals: satisfactory fracture alignment with a blurred fracture line and abundant cloud-like callus formation surrounding the site (red arrow). This image exemplifies the characteristic “rapid and hyperplastic” callus formation ability in OI, indicating successful initial healing and meeting the criteria for harness removal.

caption_evidence.quote:
Figure 8
Radiographic outcome at the final follow-up (day 136 of life). Final follow-up radiograph of the right femur demonstrates complete bony union with remodeling and consolidation of the previously formed callus (red arrow). Despite fracture healing, the underlying bony deformity and bowing of the femur persist. This image shows the final outcome of the fracture and underscores the persistent nature of the skeletal abnormalities in OI, which coexist with the fracture healing process.
